name: Tumescent liposculpture

lead: Tumescent liposculpture removes localised fat deposits with thin cannulas after the area is filled with a large volume of dilute local anaesthetic. The aim is shape rather than weight loss: a slimmer waist, a sharper jaw and neck line, or more defined abdominal muscles.

Surgeons describe the technique as carving contours, with variations such as superficial work of the face and neck and abdominal etching. Studies include randomized comparisons of adjuncts such as external ultrasound and laser-assisted lipolysis, and reviews describe a field refined over several decades.

paras: It is performed by a trained physician. The tumescent solution (dilute lidocaine with epinephrine) swells and numbs the area, a cannula is passed through small incisions to suction fat, and patients typically wear compression afterwards while swelling settles over weeks to months.

Reported complications include bleeding, infection, seroma, contour irregularities, skin damage, fluid shifts, lidocaine toxicity and, rarely, clots, fat embolism or organ perforation. Wikipedia cites about one death per ten thousand cases as of 2011, and risk rises with larger volumes and combined surgeries [1].

chain: Tumescent solution numbs and firms the fat
Slimmer waist, sharper jaw and neck, more visible muscle lines
angle.text: The procedure removes fat cells from the treated area, changing contour directly. People use it for waist, flank, jawline and abdominal definition; it is described as a shaping procedure and not as weight loss [1].

lead: Tumescent liposculpture is liposuction performed with the tumescent technique, in which the target area is infused with a large volume of dilute local anaesthetic and a vasoconstrictor until the tissue is swollen and firm, after which fat is removed through a thin cannula [1]. The term liposculpture emphasises body contouring: the American dermatologist Jeffrey Klein is credited with publishing the tumescent method in the 1980s, while Arpad and Giorgio Fischer in Rome in the 1970s used a blunt suction cannula and called their approach liposculpture [1].

For appearance, people use it to reduce stubborn localised fat that diet and exercise leave behind, to slim the waist, flanks, hips and thighs, and to define the jaw and neck. Surgeons also describe abdominal etching, which accentuates muscle contours [1]. Published studies include randomized comparisons of external ultrasound and of laser-assisted lipolysis as adjuncts, and reviews and case series on superficial liposculpture of the face, neck, trunk and gluteal region [2][3][4][5][6].

paras: In the tumescent technique the surgeon infuses a dilute mixture of lidocaine, epinephrine and sodium bicarbonate into the fat. The word tumescent means swollen and firm. The fluid numbs the tissue, limits bleeding and makes fat easier to aspirate with a cannula connected to suction [1].

Variants described in the surgical literature include syringe liposculpture, in which fat is drawn out by hand-held syringe [7]; superficial or three-dimensional liposculpture of the hips, flanks and thighs [4]; of the abdomen, waist and flanks [5]; and of the face and neck [6]. Laser neck and jowl liposculpture combined fat vaporisation with skin resurfacing [8].

People interested in jawline and neck definition, a lean waist or visible abdominal lines consider liposculpture as a surgical option for fat that remains after weight loss. Surgeons treat the abdomen with high-definition techniques that outline muscle [1].

A randomized side-by-side trial in 30 patients compared tumescent liposculpture with and without external ultrasound [2]. Three pilot studies of laser-assisted lipolysis found that a 1,064 nm laser gave no significant improvement over tumescent liposculpture alone, while a combined 1,064/1,320 nm device appeared to show some benefit [3]. A retrospective review covering 20 years of superficial three-dimensional liposculpture described hips, flanks and thighs [4]. Registered trials include cold versus warm tumescent solution in arm liposculpture and tranexamic acid in the tumescent solution to reduce bruising [9][10].

Serious complications described for liposuction include deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation, bleeding and infection, fat entering the bloodstream, and lidocaine toxicity, which ranges from ringing in the ears to convulsions; others include seroma, skin necrosis, fluid imbalance and body-shape deformity [1]. Swelling can last weeks to months, scars usually fade and altered sensation commonly recovers over several weeks [1].
Cosmetic liposuction reshapes contour and is not a weight-loss treatment. Fat can return after surgery and tends to redistribute, mostly to the abdomen [1].

timeline.event: Arpad and Giorgio Fischer in Rome use a blunt suction cannula and call it liposculpture [1].
Jeffrey A. Klein publishes the tumescent method using dilute lidocaine and epinephrine [1].
Superficial liposculpture of the face and neck is described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery [6].
A randomized trial examines external ultrasound combined with tumescent liposculpture [2].
Pilot studies compare laser-assisted lipolysis wavelengths against tumescent liposculpture [3].
A 20-year review of three-dimensional superficial liposculpture of hips, flanks and thighs is published [4].
